title: The Third Night: Discard Other People's Tasks
coreMove: Sort choice, effort, outcome, and evaluation until approval and disappointment are no longer smuggled into your jurisdiction.
sourcePressure: The source supports this as the boundary chapter: not living to satisfy expectations, separating tasks, reducing interpersonal strain through responsibility clarity, recognition hunger as unfreedom, and holding the cards in relationships.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version treats task separation as caring less; the chapter instead asks for care without control and responsibility without approval addiction.

sourceAnchors.name: How to Separate Tasks
sourceAnchors.detail: The frozen source lists this as a visible heading in the third night.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The clean question is not who feels most anxious, but who owns the choice, the effort, and the verdict.

sourceAnchors.name: Desire for Recognition Makes You Unfree
sourceAnchors.detail: The frozen source lists this as a visible heading in the third night and the sidecar says recognition hunger produces dependence and unfreedom.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: When praise becomes permission, your life has already moved into someone else's hands.

counterintuition: The kind thing is to let go
examples: generic email rewrite to please manager

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.audience: a parent tempted to manage essays, deadlines, and emotional reactions for a seventeen-year-old
exampleSpecs.stakes: the application may be polished while the teenager never owns the choice or the consequences
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Mathieu moves the laptop back across the kitchen table and says the deadline reminder is his task, but the essay choice and the admissions verdict belong to his daughter.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The application portal countdown glows beside an untouched bowl of soup.

exampleSpecs.audience: an engineering lead who wants to control whether executives blame her team after an outage
exampleSpecs.stakes: a useful postmortem may become reputation management if approval and evaluation are not separated
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 9:42 p.m., Rachel deletes the defensive slide and replaces it with the exact actions her team owns, leaving executive interpretation out of the incident timeline.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 9:42 p.m., Rachel is staring at a slide titled 'Context' that is really an apology in disguise.

exampleSpecs.audience: a bride trying to control relatives' disappointment while keeping a small ceremony
exampleSpecs.stakes: the guest list may expand until the ceremony no longer reflects the couple's real limits
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Giulia tells her aunt the invitation decision is hers and the disappointment is not, while still speaking with warmth and leaving room for the aunt's feeling.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "I understand that you're hurt," Giulia says, with the seating chart folded under her palm.

exampleSpecs.audience: a nonprofit treasurer who keeps softening numbers to protect a major donor's opinion
exampleSpecs.stakes: the board may approve a budget built to satisfy recognition rather than reality
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Thomas highlights the red deficit line, names the donor's reaction as the donor's task, and presents the real number without padding the story for approval.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The highlighter squeaks over the same red deficit line for the third time.

exampleSpecs.audience: a trades supervisor who wants to rescue an apprentice from failing by negotiating the examiner's judgment
exampleSpecs.stakes: the apprentice may pass this time while never learning which work quality is actually his to own
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Aanya stop herself from arguing with the examiner and instead put the failed conduit bend on the bench so the apprentice can own the next practice run.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can see the kink in the conduit before anyone says a word.

exampleSpecs.audience: a roommate who keeps cleaning everyone's mess to avoid being disliked
exampleSpecs.stakes: a shared apartment is becoming a silent recognition bargain rather than a livable agreement
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Pavel leaves the pan unwashed, writes his own task on the fridge chart, and lets his roommates' judgment remain theirs without staging martyrdom.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Whose opinion are you cleaning for when the pan was never yours?

skillTargets: separate choice, effort, outcome, and evaluation in a live conflict
detect when concern has become control over another person's task
identify recognition hunger as a freedom problem, not a mood problem
choose boundary actions that preserve contribution without servility

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one conflict and label four items: my choice, my effort, their response, their judgment. Cross out the item you have been trying to own.
